assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson and Tabellini built the modern formal framework linking electoral rules, constitutions and forms of government to fiscal policy and state capacity. Besley's work on state capacity and accountability complements it. The work created a research field, led to extensive empirical testing, and bears on how institutions shape policy and development.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the core pair (The Economic Effects of Constitutions, Political Economics). Besley is a clear third through state-capacity and political-agency models. Others such as Alesina, Acemoglu and Dixit are outside this credited set, so the three-name limit leaves some credit gaps.
assessment.maturity: The main contributions date from the mid-1990s to the 2010s and have been tested for decades. The field is mature, and the three-person set is coherent.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize recognised institutions and prosperity, so the committee may judge adjacent political economy as partly covered.
The field is wide and the attribution boundary (Alesina, Acemoglu, Dixit and others) is contestable.
Under the common criteria, my own field proximity should not count as merit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Melitz's heterogeneous-firm trade model transformed international trade. Selection, productivity and reallocation became central to the analysis of the gains from trade, and the framework supports a large body of empirical and quantitative work. It is the standard successor to the Krugman new-trade paradigm, which was already recognised.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the key single contribution. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, extended it to exporting versus FDI and to the integration of trade and firm-level microdata. Redding is credited here but is more of a second-generation quantitative contributor. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not in this set, which complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation across many countries' firm-level data, with wide adoption in policy analysis.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to include Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, which the three-name limit prevents.
Helpman's other work (B027) overlaps, so the credit scope is ambiguous.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities underpins how central banks model and conduct monetary policy. Calvo contributed time-dependent price setting. Taylor contributed staggered contracts and the policy rule. Woodford contributed the rigorous synthesis and the normative theory of policy.
assessment.attribution: The credited set has eight names, so any three-person selection leaves out important contributors (Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets, and others such as Clarida). The chosen trio covers the conceptual foundations best, but the credit is diffuse and contestable.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been in use for decades and was tested through the 2008 crisis, the zero lower bound and the post-pandemic inflation. It is clearly mature.
uncertainties: Heavy attribution dispersion makes a clean three-person award difficult.
Performance of the framework in the 2021-23 inflation episode is debated.
Part of the macro-modeling credit overlaps with earlier laureates (Lucas, Prescott, Kydland, Sargent, Sims, Phelps).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance made legal origins and investor protection central to the study of financial development, corporate governance and growth. It created a major research agenda in comparative institutions and finance, and it is highly cited.
assessment.attribution: The core is the La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny (LLSV) group. Shleifer is the common thread across the work. Vishny is credited in the list but would have to be dropped under the three-name limit, which is a real attribution gap.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 1997-2008, with long-run replication and critique. Debate on its causal interpretation has matured the field.
uncertainties: The causal claims about legal origins and the construction of the anti-director index have been criticised on measurement and identification.
Shleifer's non-scientific controversies, which are not part of the evidence in the supplied list, may matter to some members.
Dropping Vishny leaves a gap in credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based approach to technology and the China-shock evidence changed how economists understand labour demand, polarisation, wage inequality and the local costs of trade. The work has major policy relevance and a broad empirical footprint.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both strands. Hanson is central to the trade-shock work (with Dorn and Autor). Katz contributed the long-run skill-demand and education-race analysis. Acemoglu, Goldin and Card are already recognised for related themes, and Dorn is excluded by the name limit.
assessment.maturity: The work spans 1998 to 2020 and is widely replicated, though the task framework continues to evolve with AI and automation.
uncertainties: Contested interpretation of the China-shock findings and their external validity.
Credit overlap with Acemoglu (2024) and Goldin (2023).
Excluding Dorn is a judgement call.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income series built from tax data changed the empirical foundations of inequality research and public debate. The work extends to wealth distribution and offshore wealth, with direct implications for taxation policy.
assessment.attribution: The trio is a natural unit: Piketty and Saez pioneered the top-income series, and Zucman extended the work to wealth and tax havens. Atkinson, who died in 2017, was another foundational figure and cannot be credited.
assessment.maturity: Series have been used and revised for two decades. Contributions are well established as data infrastructure, though the theoretical claims are more contested.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of distributional national accounts, wealth estimates and capital-share dynamics.
Mixed evidence on r > g as a causal mechanism.
Policy advocacy may colour views of the scientific contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The use of population-scale administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility and the effects of neighbourhoods transformed empirical public economics and policy design. The data and methods have spread widely in the discipline.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader. Hendren and Friedman are major co-authors, but the credit is concentrated and the group is collaborative. Katz is credited here, but his contributions are already counted under B038.
assessment.maturity: Most of the key work dates from 2014 onward. The influence is large but the timeline is shorter, and long-run validation of some neighbourhood and policy findings is still underway.
uncertainties: Relatively recent. The committee may wait for further validation, as with other recent empirical contributions.
Replication and methodological debates over the neighbourhood-effects estimates.
Chetty's work spans several other candidate topics (B041), which complicates credit scope.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework showed how input distortions across firms can explain a large share of cross-country income differences. It opened a productivity research programme linking micro data to aggregate outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper. Restuccia and Rogerson, in related work, are not in the credited names, and Restuccia is credited but leaves a gap if left out under the three-name limit.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from about 2008-2009, with extensive application. Measurement critiques have refined rather than overturned the approach.
uncertainties: The size of the measured misallocation depends on assumptions about measurement error and markups.
Attribution relative to Restuccia and Rogerson is contestable.
Overlap with the growth and development ground covered by recent prizes.
